body: {"total":7,"records":[{"title":"Routine caregiver burden screening at a memory clinic followed by social work referral: a controlled before-after study","authors":"Ellison-Adeyemi F, Carvalho-Nyberg J, Obi-Hartley S","year":2022,"venue":"Journal of Dementia Care Services","doi":"10.5555/jdcs.2022.0118","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"One memory clinic introduced routine burden screening of family caregivers at the first visit and every six months, with social work referral for high scores; a second clinic continued usual care. Among 310 caregivers followed for 12 months, burden scores (0 to 48) fell by a mean of 3.1 points in the screening clinic and 0.8 points in the comparison clinic. A positive depression screen was less common at 12 months in the screening clinic (24 against 33 percent). Moves of the person with dementia to a care home did not differ. Clinics differed in staffing and caseload."},{"title":"Screening family caregivers of people with dementia: a systematic review of screening tools and their measurement properties","authors":"Marchetti-Owusu A, Lindahl-Bakare P","year":2019,"venue":"Dementia Care Evidence Reviews","doi":"10.5555/dcer.2019.0071","providerType":"review","abstract":"We identified 23 studies evaluating nine caregiver burden screening tools. Most tools correlated moderately with depression and quality of life measures, and short versions of 4 to 12 items performed similarly to longer ones. Cut-off scores for high burden varied between studies and settings. No included study tested whether screening itself, as opposed to the tools' measurement properties, changed caregiver outcomes. Few studies included caregivers who were not spouses or who spoke a language other than the tool's original language."},{"title":"Multicomponent support for dementia caregivers identified through specialist services: a randomised trial","authors":"Kawashima-Doyle T, Afolabi-Strand R, Petersen-Iwu M","year":2021,"venue":"Caregiver Support Trials","doi":"10.5555/cst.2021.0027","providerType":"Randomized Controlled Trial","abstract":"We randomised 256 caregivers with high burden scores, identified in three specialist dementia services, to six months of multicomponent support (counselling, skills training and respite planning) or to usual care. Burden scores fell by 4.2 points with support and 1.5 points with usual care at six months. At 24 months, 21 percent of people with dementia in the support group and 27 percent in the usual-care group had moved to a care home, a difference with a wide confidence interval. The trial tested support for screened caregivers, not screening itself."},{"title":"Who is missed by caregiver burden screening? Language, relationship and gender in a memory clinic","authors":"Duarte-Mensah L, Haugen-Okafor B","year":2024,"venue":"Journal of Dementia Care Services","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We examined which of 480 family caregivers attending a memory clinic completed a burden screen. Screening was completed for 86 percent of spouses and 64 percent of adult children, who attended visits less often. Only 41 percent of caregivers with limited English completed the screen, mainly because translated versions were not available. Men reported lower burden scores than women but more often declined referral when their score was high. The authors recommend offering screening outside visits and in the caregiver's language."},{"title":"Referral uptake after caregiver screening in specialist dementia services","authors":"Brightman-Oyelowo K, Salazar-Lund E","year":2020,"venue":"Social Work in Health Care Settings","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Across four specialist dementia services, we followed 390 caregivers referred to support after a high burden score. Only 38 percent attended the support service within three months. Uptake was higher when the referring clinician named a contact person and introduced the service on the same day (52 percent) than when a leaflet was given (24 percent). Caregivers who did not attend most often cited lack of time and the difficulty of leaving the person with dementia alone. Referral uptake was not recorded by relationship to the person with dementia."},{"title":"Caregiver burden and time to care home admission of people with dementia: a cohort study","authors":"Nieminen-Achebe S, Ford-Takahashi D","year":2016,"venue":"Dementia Epidemiology Letters","doi":"10.5555/del.2016.0093","providerType":"cohort","abstract":"We followed 1,140 people with dementia and their family caregivers from diagnosis for up to five years. High caregiver burden at diagnosis was associated with earlier admission of the person with dementia to a care home (hazard ratio 1.46, 95 percent CI 1.21 to 1.76) after adjustment for dementia severity, age and living arrangements. Burden was measured only once, and changes in burden over time were not captured. The association does not show that reducing burden would delay admission, because families under strain may also differ in resources and in their wishes about care."},{"title":"Screening and support for family caregivers in memory services: a regional service evaluation","authors":"Regional Memory Services Network","year":null,"venue":"Regional service evaluation report","providerType":"report","abstract":"This report describes a regional program in which memory services offered burden screening to family caregivers at diagnosis. Of 1,900 caregivers screened, 12 percent scored in the high burden range and were offered referral. The report describes how the program was organised, staff training and the referral pathways used. Caregiver outcomes were not measured, and the report does not state when the evaluation took place or how caregivers were selected for screening. Staff described the time needed to discuss scores as the main barrier to routine use."}]}
